title: George Floyd Response - 'Dominate the Streets' Military Crackdown
description_short: George Floyd Response - 'Dominate the Streets' Military Crackdown
description_medium: On June 1, 2020, President Donald Trump urged governors to deploy the National Guard in enough numbers to “dominate the streets” during protests after George Floyd’s killing. He said he would deploy federal military forces if governors did not act. In a June 12 interview, Trump said many protesters were following the crowd. These remarks document his public position, but do not identify who directed specific police tactics at Lafayette Square.
description_long: After George Floyd was killed by Minneapolis police on May 25, 2020, protests spread across the United States. In a Rose Garden address on June 1, President Donald Trump urged governors to deploy the National Guard in sufficient numbers to “dominate the streets.” He said that if local officials did not act, he would deploy federal military forces to respond. At the time, police had used force to clear protesters from the area near Lafayette Square before Trump walked to St. John’s Church. The supplied reporting documents Trump’s statement and the surrounding protest response, but it does not establish that he ordered the specific tactics used in the clearing or identify who made those operational decisions. In a June 12 interview, Trump also said many people protesting Floyd’s death were following the crowd and did not know why they were there. The remarks framed a nationwide protest movement primarily through the lens of public order and possible military deployment. They show a conditional threat and public characterization of demonstrators, not a completed federal troop deployment. The sources do not establish the later effects of those remarks on police operations or protest participation.

title: Ends DED for Liberians with One-Year Wind-Down
description_short: Ends DED for Liberians with One-Year Wind-Down
description_medium: On March 27, 2018, Donald Trump directed the termination of Deferred Enforced Departure for Liberian beneficiaries, with the program ending March 31, 2019. The order allowed a 12-month wind-down and continued work authorization for eligible people who had lived continuously in the United States since October 1, 2002. The memorandum cited improved conditions in Liberia while providing transition time for affected residents.
description_long: A presidential memorandum issued on March 27, 2018, directed the termination of Deferred Enforced Departure for Liberian beneficiaries effective March 31, 2019. DED had allowed eligible Liberians to remain in the United States when they otherwise could have been removed. The memorandum said that Liberia had made progress in restoring stability and democratic governance and had recovered from the Ebola outbreak; on that basis, the administration concluded that conditions no longer warranted another extension. It nevertheless established a 12-month wind-down beginning March 31, 2018. Eligible beneficiaries who had continuously lived in the United States since October 1, 2002, could remain during that period and retain work authorization. The transition did not apply to certain people excluded under immigration law. The order gave affected residents a year before the termination date, but it did not extend the protection beyond March 2019. The supplied memorandum sets out the administration’s rationale and transition terms; it does not describe how many people were affected or what happened to individuals after the wind-down ended. Those outcomes require separate records.

title: Pardons Patrick Lee Swisher
description_medium: The Justice Department lists Patrick Lee Swisher among Donald Trump’s pardon recipients. Swisher was sentenced in the Western District of North Carolina to 30 months in prison, two years of supervised release, and a $5,000 fine for filing a fraudulent tax return or statement and making false statements. The supplied record does not give an individualized reason for the pardon.
description_long: Donald Trump granted Patrick Lee Swisher a presidential pardon on May 24, 2018, according to the supplied entry and the Justice Department’s pardon list. Swisher’s case was in the Western District of North Carolina. The DOJ record lists a sentence of 30 months in prison, two years of supervised release, and a $5,000 fine, imposed in 2002. The listed offenses were filing a fraudulent tax return or statement and making false statements. The official clemency record confirms the pardon and the underlying case information, but it does not provide an individualized explanation for why Swisher was selected or describe any consequences beyond the grant of clemency. A pardon is distinct from a commutation: it is an act of executive clemency and does not erase the historical fact of the conviction. The supplied materials do not establish any connection between Swisher and Trump or the administration. The event can therefore be described as a pardon for a person convicted of tax-related and false-statement offenses, without inferring a personal relationship or an improper motive.

title: Pardons Carl Andrew Boggs, III
description_medium: The Justice Department’s clemency record identifies Carl Andrew Boggs III, also known as Drew Boggs, among the full and unconditional pardons Trump issued on January 19, 2021. Boggs had been convicted of conspiracy to commit mail and wire fraud and conspiracy to commit money laundering in the Western District of North Carolina. His sentence included 30 months in prison, two years’ supervised release, and a $15,000 fine.
description_long: On January 19, 2021, Donald Trump granted Carl Andrew Boggs III, also known as Drew Boggs, a full and unconditional pardon. The Justice Department’s clemency record lists Boggs’s convictions in the Western District of North Carolina for conspiracy to commit mail and wire fraud and conspiracy to commit money laundering. It records a 2015 sentence of 30 months in prison, two years of supervised release, and a $15,000 fine. Boggs was included in the group of pardons announced on Trump’s final day in office. The official record confirms the pardon and offenses it covered but gives no individualized reason for the decision. A pardon is executive clemency; it does not erase the historical fact of the conviction or operate as a court ruling that reverses it.
